newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Wider band raised NZ inflation expectations - ANZ.
newsitem.headline: Wider band raised NZ inflation expectations - ANZ.

text.p: ANZ Bank said on Monday there was some evidence that the widening of the Reserve Bank's inflation target and greater government spending has raised inflation expectations.

ANZ said it is too early to say what impact the policy changes have had on public inflation expectations but an analysis of the different yields of indexed and non-indexed bonds in the money markets suggested the financial market's long-term inflation expectations had risen by around 0.5 percent.

"To the extent a wider target does act to increase long-term inflation expectations, monetary policy will generally have to be tighter over time than would otherwise have been necessary," ANZ said in its weekly Focus publication.
The bank noted that Reserve Bank governor Don Brash has said there is a risk that the higher mid-point in the new target could increase public inflation expectations.
If the public perceived the bank was trying to maintain inflation at the top end of the new 0-3 percent target expectations could increase a full one percent, ANZ said.
Last year's coalition government agreement widened the target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent and included NZ$5 billion of extra spending over five years.

ANZ said the yield between the inflation indexed February 2016 and the longest dated government bond of November 2006 increased from 2.0 percent to around 2.5 percent during December, co-inciding with the widening of the target.
ANZ said it had to borne in mind that there few inflation indexed bonds on issue and other factors acted on them.

"Nevertheless, while these inflation index bond factors may explain a portion of the increase in the ordinary/index bond yield spread, the increase in this spread, and its timing, suggests the financial markets's long-term inflation expectations have risen following the widening of the RBNZ's inflation target band and the announcement of increased government expenditure."
